messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That might refer to the standard error of the mean under null? Usually we compute standard error: sigma / sqrt(n). But they gave sample standard deviation 1.4. For null hypothesis test, we might use sample standard deviation as estimate of population standard deviation. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40). Let's compute: sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2213. So standard error ~0.221.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under null: that's the standard error. So answer: about 0.221.

Alternatively, if they want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test statistic? That would be the standard error of the difference between sample mean and population mean? Actually the test statistic t = (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is the standard error. So standard deviation of the null distribution of t is 1 (for t distribution with df=39). But they ask "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" which is ambiguous. They might want the standard error of the mean. So I'd answer 0.221.
